feed.title: Game Development — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Awesome Babylon.js
entry.summary: A resource list for Babylon.js, a 3D game engine for web and native. Unlike Three.js it behaves like an engine rather than a rendering library: physics integration, the Inspector and the Playground come built in.

entry.title: Awesome Flame
entry.summary: A resource list for Flame, the game engine for Flutter. Unlike general Flutter lists, it focuses only on game development — Flame plugins, sample games, tutorials.

entry.title: Awesome Game Boy Dev
entry.summary: Game development for the Game Boy — assemblers, tools and hardware docs. Unlike modern engine lists it focuses on programming constrained retro hardware.

entry.title: Awesome Game Development
entry.summary: A resource list covering every branch of game development from engines to asset tools. Unlike engine-specific lists it is engine-agnostic — a broad starting map.

entry.title: Awesome Game Engine Dev
entry.summary: Resources for writing the game engine itself, not a game — rendering, physics, ECS. Unlike engine-usage lists it aims at building an engine from scratch.

entry.title: Awesome Game Remakes
entry.summary: A list of actively maintained, open-source remakes of classic games. Unlike emulators the game’s engine has been rewritten from scratch — the code is readable.

entry.title: Awesome Games of Coding
entry.summary: A list of games that teach a programming language by making games. Unlike dry exercises it ties learning to a game’s progression.

entry.title: Awesome Godot
entry.summary: A list of plugins, tutorials and example projects for the open-source Godot engine. Unlike the official docs it gathers the tools and templates the community produced.

entry.title: Awesome Learn Gamedev
entry.summary: Course, book and community resources for learning to make games. Unlike tool lists it offers an ordered path and also covers side crafts like art, audio and design.

entry.title: Awesome libGDX
entry.summary: A list of libraries and resources for libGDX, the Java game framework that targets desktop, Android, iOS and web from one codebase. Unlike Unity lists, it centres on a code-first framework rather than an editor.

entry.title: Awesome LÖVE2D
entry.summary: A list of resources and libraries for LÖVE, the Lua-based game engine. Unlike engines with an editor such as Godot, it has none — everything is Lua code; the list gathers the libraries that fill that gap.

entry.title: Awesome Minecraft
entry.summary: A list gathering Minecraft server software, mods, launchers and tools. Unlike the official wiki, it covers the software ecosystem around the game rather than the game itself.

entry.title: Awesome Open Source Games
entry.summary: A list of playable games whose source is open. Unlike game stores these are projects whose code you can read to learn how they were made and build on.

entry.title: Awesome OpenGL
entry.summary: A list of libraries and tutorials for OpenGL, the 2D/3D rendering API. Unlike Vulkan it is higher-level and easier to learn — still the most common way into graphics programming.

entry.title: Awesome PICO-8
entry.summary: A list of games and tools for PICO-8, the retro-constrained fantasy console. Unlike general game engines, it has you build within deliberate limits — a 128×128 screen, 16 colours.

entry.title: Awesome Vulkan
entry.summary: A resource list for Vulkan, the low-overhead 3D graphics and compute API. Unlike OpenGL it hands you the work the driver used to do — memory management, synchronisation: faster, but far more verbose.

entry.title: Catlike Coding
entry.summary: Rigorous, step-by-step Unity C# tutorial series that reach advanced topics such as a custom render pipeline and procedural meshes. Unlike video tutorials it is written, and explains why the code does what it does at every step.

entry.title: Game Developer
entry.summary: Formerly Gamasutra — industry articles and game-development postmortems.

entry.title: itch.io
entry.summary: An open, pay-what-you-want marketplace for indie games, tools and assets.

entry.title: Kenney
entry.summary: Cohesive, huge CC0 game-asset packs, free and unrestricted to use. Unlike community archives such as OpenGameArt, they come from one hand, so each pack shares a single style.

entry.title: LearnOpenGL
entry.summary: A comprehensive, well-ordered tutorial teaching modern OpenGL from scratch.

entry.title: LÖVE
entry.summary: A Lua framework for 2D games, well suited to fast prototyping.

entry.title: MagicTools
entry.summary: A list of tools and resources for game and graphics development — sprites, tiles, audio, level editors. Unlike engine lists it focuses on the helper tools in the production pipeline.

entry.title: OpenGameArt
entry.summary: A community library of freely licensed (CC) game art and audio.

entry.title: Phaser
entry.summary: An HTML5 game framework for building 2D web games in JavaScript.

entry.title: raylib
entry.summary: A simple, beginner-friendly C library for games that gets you started fast.

entry.title: Red Blob Games
entry.summary: Tutorials explaining game-dev maths — A*, hex grids, field of view — through interactive visuals. Unlike textbooks, you watch the algorithm by playing with it on the page.

entry.title: The Book of Shaders
entry.summary: A gentle, interactive introduction to fragment shaders (GLSL).

entry.title: Game Programming Patterns
entry.summary: Robert Nystrom’s free book on the design patterns that recur in game code. Unlike general design-pattern books its examples are specific to the game loop and performance.

entry.title: Unity
entry.summary: The most widely used cross-platform game engine; 2D/3D, mobile and console. Unlike Godot it has a huge asset store and industry ubiquity — most job listings ask for it.
